# Threat model

This crate decides whether a machine should install a release. It stops a
set of attacks that a single signing key does not, and it leaves others
open. This page says which is which, so that you can decide whether it is
enough for your project before you sign your first root.

It cannot tell a good release from a bad one. It can only tell whether
enough of the people your root names signed this release, for this
machine, and recently. If those people sign something harmful, or sign
something a compromised build server made, the crate verifies it.

Every claim below names the section of
[the release-metadata decision](decisions/architecture/delivery/release-metadata.md)
it rests on, written §1 to §8. "Context" is the decision's section on what a
verifier must stop.

## What it stops

A machine downloads releases from servers it does not trust: a mirror, a
CDN, a cache, a network someone else controls. The attacks below are the
ones the TUF specification names, plus one for audiences (Context).

- **A file you never released.** Every artifact's length and hashes are in a
  signed record, so one changed byte fails the check (§1).
- **An old release, correctly signed.** Every record has a version, and a
  machine never accepts a version lower than one it already trusts, so an
  attacker cannot send it back to a release with a known defect (§1).
- **Records from two different releases served together.** One signed
  record lists the version of every other record, so a machine reads them
  only in combinations that existed (§1).
- **A release for one audience installed by another.** Each audience, such
  as `stable` or `beta`, is its own role with its own signers and its own
  threshold, and a target's path names its audience. A release signed for
  testers does not install on a machine that takes only stable releases
  (§2).
- **One stolen key.** Each record needs a threshold of signatures, and the
  threshold counts people, not keys. A maintainer who holds a laptop key, a
  security key and a phone passkey is one signatory, so one person cannot
  meet a threshold of two however many of their keys they use (§4). The
  same public key listed twice, under two names, is refused, so it cannot
  count twice either (§4).
- **The build server, taken over.** The only release key on the build
  server signs freshness: the snapshot and the timestamp. A thief with it
  cannot make a machine accept an artifact that a maintainer did not sign
  (§6).
- **A signature made for something else.** Every signature is made under
  a fixed namespace, `release-metadata` for one file and
  `release-metadata-batch` for several, so a git commit signature or a
  file signature that a maintainer's key made does not count as a release
  signature (§3). A signature over several files counts on a file only
  when its statement names that file's role, version and body hash, so it
  cannot be moved to another file or another version (§3).
- **A forged change of signers.** A new root counts only when enough
  signers of the root a machine already trusts sign it, and enough signers
  of the new root sign it too. A machine that missed several versions checks
  each in turn. So adding a signer, removing one or replacing a lost key
  needs the people the machines already trust (§5).
- **A signature made without a touch, where you demanded one.** A signer's
  rule can demand that a security key or passkey signature shows a person
  touched the device, or that the device checked a PIN or a biometric. A
  signature without the flag does not count for that signer (§4).

## What it does not stop

**A compromised build, where the build is not reproducible.** A build
server that an attacker controls can produce a bad artifact and a correct
record of it. If your build is reproducible, each signer rebuilds the
artifact from the tagged source on their own machine, and the signing
command refuses to sign when the rebuild differs, so a threshold of two
signers is also two independent builds. If it is not, the signer says so
with `--not-reproducible`, and the signatures then show who approved the
release, not how it was built (§6). Even a reproducible build only shows
that the artifact matches the tagged source; a harmful commit in that
source passes, because the rebuild starts from it (§6).

**A freeze, until the timestamp expires.** Someone who controls what a
machine downloads, or who stole the build server's freshness key, can keep
serving the last records the machine already trusts. The machine keeps
installing nothing new until the timestamp expires, and then it knows it
is behind (§1, §6). How long that takes is the timestamp's lifetime, which
you choose; the scheme fixes no number (§1).

**Losing more root keys than the root's threshold.** If more root keys are
lost than the threshold allows, nobody can sign a new root, and every user
must replace the root by hand. Set the root's threshold and the number of
root keys with that in mind (decision, Consequences).

**A quorum acting in bad faith.** Enough signers acting together can sign
any release and any new root, and the crate verifies it. Thresholds count
people; they cannot judge what those people intend (§4). Where a key is
kept, a security key, a Secure Enclave, a phone, a file, is a claim the root
makes, not something the crate can prove (§4).

**The first root.** A machine's trust starts at the root it got with the
software (§1). Whatever delivered that software delivered the root, and
nothing in this scheme checks that delivery. For a machine already
installed before you adopt this scheme, that is the update which first
carries the root: it arrives through your old update path, unchecked by
this one. After that hop, every change is checked.

**An approval given before the build.** Signers can approve a release
before it exists by delegating one version's files to a key that a build
session made, for at most a day; the session signs the artifact when it is
ready (§8). The signers do not see the final artifact, and any program on
that session's machine can use the key until the delegation expires (§8).
The crate cannot see that the pattern names only one version, or that the
session made the key: the signers check both before they sign, and the
`status` command shows each delegation's pattern and key id so that they
can (§8). The 24-hour limit is checked when the delegation is staged, not
by the verifier, because the records carry no start time (§8). For an
audience the root marks public, the delegation needs every signer of that
audience, not just its threshold (§8).

**Stock TUF clients, on a root signed with hardware keys.** The record
format is TUF's, and a root whose keys all use TUF's own `ed25519` scheme,
one key per signer, reads the same in other TUF clients (§4). Security
keys, Secure Enclave keys and passkeys sign SSHSIG envelopes, which other
TUF clients do not verify, so a root they sign verifies only in this crate
(§3, §4).

**A signature without a touch, where you did not demand one.** A security
key's signature counts whether or not it shows a touch, unless the signer's
rule demands it. If you want a touch on every release, put it in your
rule (§4).

## What it assumes

- **Root keys stay offline and sign only roots.** The keys that sign the
  root and the releases are on the maintainers' devices, never on the build
  server, and the root's keys sign nothing but roots (§5, §6).
- **The online key signs only freshness.** The one key on the build server
  signs the snapshot and the timestamp, and no role lists it for releases
  (§6).
- **The first root is pinned at install.** Each machine gets its first
  root with the software, and trusts nothing before it (§1).
- **Signers read what they sign.** The records are canonical JSON, and a
  change is reviewed as a text diff before each signer signs it (§1). The
  signing commands sign only through the signer program you name, such as
  `ssh-keygen`, and hold no key themselves (§7).
- **The machine's clock is roughly right.** The verifier reads no clock;
  the program that embeds it passes the current time (§7). A machine whose
  clock runs far behind keeps accepting records that have expired.
- **Fetching is yours.** The crate opens no connection. The program that
  embeds it fetches the records and the artifact, and a machine that
  cannot fetch keeps the state it trusts (§7).
